notes: CBV-TP is the pharmacologically active antiviral metabolite; hepatic elimination occurs via alcohol dehydrogenase and glucuronyl transferase to inactive metabolites. Liver injury is primarily HLA-B*57:01-linked hypersensitivity (LiverTox NBK548225).

Prodrug rapidly hydrolyzed in vivo to active CYP17 inhibitor abiraterone; LiverTox (NBK548136) notes further hepatic metabolism by CYP3A4/CYP2D6 may form an uncharacterized toxic or immunogenic intermediate.

Minimally absorbed (<2% as active drug) and metabolized exclusively in the GI tract; <2% of an active glucose-cleavage product is recovered in urine (DailyMed) and PMC6090209 concludes acarbose does not cause hepatotoxicity via its metabolites.

injury_mechanism: Depletes hepatic glutathione in overdose and covalently binds intracellular macromolecules and cysteine residues causing centrilobular hepatocellular necrosis and apoptosis.
notes: Classic dose-dependent intrinsic hepatotoxin; CYP2E1 is the primary bioactivating enzyme.
No active or toxic liver metabolite identified; rare liver injury is believed to be idiosyncratic sulfonamide-like hypersensitivity (HLA-B*59:01 association).

Acitretin is the active metabolite of etretinate but undergoes reverse transesterification back to teratogenic/active etretinate in the presence of ethanol; mechanism of acitretin hepatotoxicity is unknown (LiverTox NBK548784).

Discontinued SSRI; abnormal liver function tests occurred in early clinical studies (PMID 6433393) and reversible CYP inhibition in humans (PMID 6519152) but no specific active or hepatotoxic metabolite is documented.
Alatrofloxacin mesylate is the intravenous prodrug rapidly hydrolyzed in vivo to the active fluoroquinolone trovafloxacin.

injury_mechanism: Uniquely induces hepatic CXCL-2 expression and mediates UGT1A1-dependent hepatocellular toxicity in vitro and in LPS-cotreated mice.
notes: Trovafloxacin was withdrawn/restricted due to severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity; UGT1A1-mediated acyl-glucuronidation is implicated in liver injury.

Rapidly converted in the liver on first pass to the primary systemic anthelmintic metabolite albendazole sulfoxide (FMO/CYP3A4 per PMC11064478); mechanism of liver enzyme elevations is unknown (LiverTox NBK548360).

injury_mechanism: Reactive epoxide intermediate forms covalent adducts with cellular nucleophiles and destroys cytochrome P450 linked to hypersensitivity and hepatotoxicity.
notes: Alclofenac epoxide was identified in human urine (PMID 6103793) and is cited as a possible cause of alclofenac hepatotoxicity (PMC1434053).

injury_mechanism: Triggers a cytotoxic T-cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity reaction (often with DRESS) strongly associated with HLA-B*58:01 causing immunoallergic hepatitis.
notes: Oxypurinol is the primary pharmacologically active xanthine oxidase inhibitor metabolite (formed by XO and AO per PMC9730672) and the suspected antigenic driver of allopurinol immunoallergic hepatitis (LiverTox NBK548098).

injury_mechanism: Depletes hepatic glutathione and forms covalent GSH/protein adducts while inducing mitochondrial permeability transition causing hepatocellular necrosis.
notes: Withdrawn due to severe hepatotoxicity; chloro-imidazopyridine ring is bioactivated by CYP1A to a reactive epoxide (also reviewed in PMC6151358).

injury_mechanism: Forms NADPH-dependent covalent microsomal protein adducts acting as a hapten to trigger immunoallergic hepatitis while its heptanoic side chain competes with mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation.
notes: Withdrawn due to prolonged cholestatic hepatitis and microvesicular steatosis; specific CYP isoform is not identified (LiverTox NBK548584).
Acetylated in the liver to inactive acetyl-PAS; hepatotoxicity is rare and attributed to idiosyncratic hypersensitivity without an established toxic metabolite.

injury_mechanism: Accumulates in hepatic tissue and inhibits phospholipase A causing phospholipidosis and mitochondrial dysfunction.
notes: DEA has antiarrhythmic activity and accumulates in the liver alongside parent amiodarone in chronic hepatotoxicity (LiverTox NBK548109); acute IV transaminitis is linked to diluent polysorbate 80 or hepatic ischemia.
Hepatic metabolism is not observed; undergoes slow non-enzymatic chemical degradation to an inactive ring-opened peptide (confirmed in LiverTox NBK548299).
Development halted in 2005 due to idiosyncratic severe hepatotoxicity; metabolized by CYP3A (minor CYP2C19) and glucuronidation but no specific active or hepatotoxic metabolite is established.
Bacterial enzyme directly toxic to hepatocytes via systemic asparagine/arginine depletion and inhibition of hepatic protein and lipoprotein synthesis; does not form small-molecule metabolites.
Main oxidative metabolite equipotent to atomoxetine as a norepinephrine transporter inhibitor.

injury_mechanism: Electrophilic quinone and aldehyde intermediates covalently modify hepatic proteins and DNA in vitro and in animal models hypothesized to contribute to idiosyncratic liver injury.
notes: Trapped as GSH/methoxyamine adducts in human and rodent liver microsomes; LiverTox (NBK548671) notes clinical mechanism of injury remains unproven.
Active metabolite with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory potency equivalent to parent atorvastatin; active metabolites account for ~70% of circulating inhibitory activity.
Active metabolite with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory potency equivalent to parent atorvastatin; active metabolites account for ~70% of circulating inhibitory activity.
Azathioprine is a prodrug cleaved to active 6-mercaptopurine which is further converted to active 6-thioguanine nucleotides.
Primary active immunosuppressive/cytotoxic nucleotides responsible for therapeutic efficacy and myelosuppression.

injury_mechanism: Accumulate in hepatocytes at high TPMT activity and cause direct dose-dependent serum aminotransferase elevations and hepatocellular injury.
notes: Also associated with nodular regenerative hyperplasia and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome; nitroimidazole moiety is separately linked to cholestatic hypersensitivity.
Main metabolite possessing radical-scavenger activity; bendazac causes idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity (PMID 7644786) with no established hepatotoxic metabolite.

injury_mechanism: Undergoes acyl migration and covalently binds hepatocellular proteins via transacylation or Schiff base formation contributing to severe cholestatic/hepatocellular injury.
notes: Withdrawn in 1982 due to fatal cholestatic jaundice; acyl glucuronide accounts for ~50% of covalent protein adducts in human and rat hepatocytes.

Parent benzarone directly uncouples oxidative phosphorylation and inhibits mitochondrial beta-oxidation causing hepatocyte apoptosis/necrosis (LiverTox NBK548732); no specific active or toxic metabolite is established.

injury_mechanism: Catechol and reactive quinone/epoxide intermediates induce mitochondrial membrane permeability transition and inhibit beta-oxidation while increasing ROS leading to hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis.
notes: Withdrawn in Europe due to severe/fatal hepatotoxicity; CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 bioactivation pathways are linked to mitochondrial toxicity (also LiverTox NBK548732).
Withdrawn uricosuric associated with jaundice; one 2023 study notes a possible metabolite (6-hydroxybenziodarone), not yet confirmed as a well-documented human clinical or hepatotoxic metabolite.
Active in vitro in retinoid receptor activation assays, though relative contribution to human efficacy/safety is unknown; LiverTox (NBK548336) notes liver injury mechanism is unknown.
DailyMed confirms R-bicalutamide is oxidized to an inactive metabolite followed by glucuronidation; LiverTox (NBK547970) states hepatotoxicity mechanism is unknown.
DailyMed confirms bortezomib is oxidatively metabolized (deboronated) to inactive metabolites; LiverTox (NBK548027) notes liver injury mechanism is unknown.

Ro 48-5033 is pharmacologically active (up to 20% of parent activity); parent bosentan exhibited hepatotoxicity (IC50 ~54 uM) in human hepatocytes whereas Ro 48-5033 showed no significant cytotoxicity.
FDA label confirms circulating metabolites M2 (oxydechlorinated), M5 (N-desmethylated), and M6 (N-oxide) are all inactive; LiverTox (NBK547951) notes cause of liver injury is unknown.

injury_mechanism: Reactive acyl glucuronide and cyclized bromfenac indolinone (lactam) metabolites cause hepatocellular cytotoxicity (34-fold higher cytotoxicity than parent bromfenac in vitro) and protein adduct formation.
notes: Withdrawn NSAID due to severe hepatotoxicity; forms bromfenac acyl glucuronide and bromfenac indolinone (lactam).

DailyMed confirms enzymatic metabolites (tetrahydrothiophene, sulfolane, 3-hydroxysulfolane) lack cytotoxic activity; LiverTox (NBK548886) attributes sinusoidal obstruction syndrome to direct parent hydrolysis/alkylation.

injury_mechanism: Forms covalent protein adducts (haptenation) and alters HLA-B*15:02 peptide binding, contributing to immune-mediated hypersensitivity hepatitis/DRESS.
notes: Pharmacologically active anticonvulsant metabolite; also implicated in covalent protein binding alongside arene oxide intermediates.

injury_mechanism: Unstable electrophilic arene oxides covalently bind hepatic proteins to form haptens, triggering immune-mediated hypersensitivity liver injury.
notes: Primary reactive intermediate pathway classically linked to anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome and DILI.

DailyMed states carfilzomib is rapidly metabolized via peptidase cleavage and epoxide hydrolysis (minor CYP role) with no active or hepatotoxic metabolites identified; LiverTox (NBK548814) notes unknown mechanism.

DailyMed confirms parent ceritinib is the main circulating component (82%) metabolized by CYP3A with no clinically important active or toxic metabolites documented; LiverTox (NBK548045) notes unknown mechanism.
Hydrolyzed/metabolized to 4-chlorobenzoic acid, 4-chlorohippuric acid, and 4-chlorobenzaldehyde derivatives; no active or hepatotoxic metabolite established in human DILI literature.

Major metabolite 6-hydroxychlorzoxazone (via CYP2E1) is pharmacologically inactive per standard monographs, though one secondary ResearchGate abstract calls it a toxic metabolite; LiverTox notes idiosyncratic injury of unknown mechanism.
Withdrawn in the 1930s due to severe acute hepatic necrosis (suspected hypersensitivity or metabolic idiosyncrasy); no specific human hepatotoxic metabolite identified.
Suspected hypersensitivity mechanism; no active or liver-toxic metabolite established.

DailyMed confirms 14-OH clarithromycin has clinically significant antimicrobial activity (2x more active than parent against H. influenzae); LiverTox (NBK547886) notes hepatotoxicity mechanism is unknown.
Withdrawn vMost-DILI-concern antipsychotic; no human active or hepatotoxic metabolites documented in preferred sources.
Withdrawn NSAID causing autoimmune-like chronic active hepatitis (anti-actin antibodies); no specific human hepatotoxic metabolite identified.
Major active metabolite (norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor); LiverTox (NBK548878) notes hepatotoxicity mechanism is unknown (possible toxic intermediate).
Major pharmacologically active circulating metabolite.

injury_mechanism: Electrophilic reactive nitrenium ion covalently binds hepatic cellular proteins (haptenation) and depletes glutathione, triggering oxidative/immune-mediated hepatotoxicity.
notes: Formed in human liver microsomes primarily via CYP3A4 (associated with hepatotoxicity and agranulocytosis).

Active metabolite referenced in DailyMed Xalkori label (2a51b0de-47d6-455e-a94c-d2c737b04ff7); 2.5- to 8-fold less potent than parent in vitro; LiverTox (NBK548638) notes hepatotoxicity mechanism is unknown.
Cyclofenil diacetate ester is hydrolyzed to its active SERM metabolite cyclofenil diphenol; no specific hepatotoxic metabolite established.
DailyMed confirms metabolites have considerably less biological activity and toxicity than parent cyclosporine; LiverTox (NBK548753) attributes cholestasis to parent drug effects on bile flow.
Intracellular active metabolite inhibiting DNA polymerase; LiverTox (NBK548291) notes hepatotoxicity is rare and likely direct parent/hepatocyte toxicity with no named hepatotoxic metabolite.

injury_mechanism: Hepatic CYP450 N-demethylation generates HMMTIC/MTIC and the reactive methyldiazonium ion, which alkylates DNA/macromolecules and injures hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells (causing sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/hepatic necrosis).
notes: Prodrug requiring hepatic CYP bioactivation for both antineoplastic alkylation and toxic metabolite generation in the liver (MDPI Int J Mol Sci 2025).

injury_mechanism: Direct toxin causing hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cell damage (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome); no active or liver-toxic metabolite documented.
notes: Likelihood score C; minimal hepatic metabolism.

injury_mechanism: C-17alpha alkylated steroid causing cholestasis and vascular/neoplastic liver lesions directly; urinary metabolites (2-hydroxymethyl danazol and ethisterone) are not documented as liver-toxic.
notes: Metabolism details also verified in StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK564344/).

Possesses muscle relaxant activity similar to parent. LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548144/) notes higher doses suggest a toxic metabolite based on animal nitroreduction studies, but no specific human hepatotoxic metabolite is established.

injury_mechanism: Extensively metabolized by CYP3A4; toxic intermediates are suspected in LiverTox but no specific named active or liver-toxic metabolite is established.
notes: Likelihood score C.

injury_mechanism: Mechanism unknown (possibly direct intrinsic toxicity exacerbated by iron overload or ABCC2 variants); no active or liver-toxic metabolite established.
notes: Likelihood score C (FDA boxed warning for hepatotoxicity).

injury_mechanism: No documented human hepatotoxic or pharmacologically active small-molecule metabolite.
notes: No LiverTox entry; endogenous/therapeutic glycosaminoglycan degraded via stepwise lysosomal catabolism.

injury_mechanism: Forms covalent protein adducts in human hepatocytes (triggering immune-mediated injury) and causes direct cytotoxicity with marked ROS generation and superoxide dismutase inhibition.
notes: Pharmacologically active (COX-1 IC50 0.620 uM, COX-2 IC50 2.91 uM) and more cytotoxic than parent diclofenac. LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547953/) notes UGT2B7/CYP2C8/ABCC2 genetic linkage and hepatic protein adducts in human DILI.

injury_mechanism: Inhibits mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma causing mtDNA depletion and impaired oxidative phosphorylation resulting in lactic acidosis and microvesicular hepatic steatosis (LASH).
notes: Active antiretroviral metabolite (HIV reverse transcriptase chain terminator) and primary mediator of mitochondrial hepatotoxicity and noncirrhotic portal hypertension; intracellular phosphorylation confirmed in Videx monograph (https://pdf.hres.ca/dpd_pm/00003392.PDF).

injury_mechanism: Human hepatotoxicity is likely hypersensitivity-mediated; no named human hepatotoxic metabolite is established.
notes: Likelihood score C. Isolated perfused rat liver studies (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9456294/) show diflunisal acyl glucuronide forms covalent liver protein adducts (animal/mechanistic only; not established in human DILI).

Present in plasma at 10-20% of parent drug with 25-50% of parent's coronary vasodilator potency. LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547898/) states hepatotoxicity is likely hypersensitivity.
Prodrug rapidly hydrolyzed to its sole active metabolite MMF (activates Nrf2 and HCAR2). LiverTox scores DMF as C and MMF as E* (unproven/suspected rare idiosyncratic DILI; mechanism unknown).

forming_enzyme: Glutathione/enzymatic reduction (to DDTC); thiol methyltransferase & CYP/FMO oxidation (to sulfoxide/sulfone)
notes: Active metabolites responsible for irreversible ALDH1A1 inhibition. LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548103/) states human hepatotoxicity is probably idiosyncratic hypersensitivity (immunoallergic with CYP1A2 autoantibodies).

injury_mechanism: Inhibits mitochondrial beta-oxidation and causes microvesicular steatosis, hyperammonemia, and Reye-like hepatotoxicity.
notes: Divalproex dissociates into valproate in the GI tract; 4-ene-VPA also has antiepileptic and HDAC-inhibiting activity. LiverTox URL: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548284/.

injury_mechanism: Reversibly binds the alpha-subunit of mitochondrial trifunctional protein to inhibit beta-oxidation and depletes acetyl-CoA/glutamate impairing NAGS/CPS1 and causing hyperammonemia and hepatotoxicity.
notes: Also undergoes glucuronidation.

injury_mechanism: Inhibits succinate-CoA ligase (causing mitochondrial DNA depletion) and N-acetylglutamate synthase (causing hyperammonemia) in hepatocytes.
notes: Also exhibits antiepileptic activity.

injury_mechanism: Metabolized primarily to an inactive ether glucuronide; hepatotoxicity mechanism is unknown (hypersensitivity/IRIS in HBV/HCV coinfection).
notes: LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548350/) likelihood score D; no active or liver-toxic metabolite established.

Major circulating active metabolite (lower potency than parent). PMC6348481 showed CYP3A4/3A5/2D6 metabolism attenuates dronedarone cytotoxicity and topoisomerase IIalpha suppression (parent is more cytotoxic); LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548208/) notes idiosyncratic DILI may involve a toxic/immunogenic intermediate.

Droxicam is a prodrug hydrolyzed to active NSAID piroxicam. LiverTox notes piroxicam (and droxicam, citing 4 cases of droxicam-induced liver injury) causes idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity possibly via a toxic metabolic intermediate or hypersensitivity.

injury_mechanism: LiverTox notes injury is likely due to a metabolic byproduct but no specific human hepatotoxic metabolite is established.
notes: Likelihood score B. Hydroxylated and epoxide metabolites triggering ROS are reported in rat studies (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7781826/; animal-only/mechanistic).

injury_mechanism: Associated with severe acute toxic hepatitis and rapid progression to cirrhosis in humans (withdrawn); no specific active or liver-toxic metabolite is established.
notes: No LiverTox entry; mechanism of human hepatotoxicity remains unestablished.

injury_mechanism: Induces ROS formation and caspase-3 activation and triggers JNK- and BimEL-dependent apoptosis in primary human hepatocytes at lower concentrations than parent efavirenz.
notes: DISAGREEMENT: Primary human hepatocyte studies (PubMed 21958719) found 8-OHEFV is more hepatotoxic than parent EFV, whereas a clinical cohort (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3232196/, n=353) found DILI associated with higher plasma parent EFV and EFV/8-OHEFV ratio (CYP2B6*6 slow metabolizers), not 8-OHEFV levels. StatPearls (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542316/) notes hydroxylated metabolites are inactive.

injury_mechanism: Forms covalent protein adducts, triggers immune activation, and undergoes enterohepatic recirculation; plasma levels >=4.0 ug/mL concentration-dependently predict human DILI.
notes: Validated in 42 human aplastic anemia patients (AUC 0.83 vs 0.68 for parent; UGT1A1 EMs 43% DILI incidence vs 11% IMs and 0% PMs). LiverTox URL: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548101/.

Major active metabolite in human plasma. PMC6191908 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6191908/) found CYP3A4 inducers increase human erlotinib hepatotoxicity 2.7-fold and notes CYP oxidation to reactive epoxide/quinone-imine intermediates (in vitro).
Propionyl ester lauryl sulfate prodrug/salt hydrolyzed in vivo to active erythromycin base. LiverTox notes estolate causes cholestatic hepatitis via hypersensitivity/immunoallergic reaction.
Major active plasma metabolite; label notes hepatic enzyme and bilirubin abnormalities occur but no hepatotoxic metabolite mechanism is established.
Major active plasma metabolite.
Active estrogenic metabolites contributing to clinical activity and endocrine effects.

injury_mechanism: Likelihood score C (often part of DRESS); mechanism unknown (likely hypersensitivity) with no active or liver-toxic metabolite documented.

notes: Likelihood score C. Stereoselective formation of etodolac acyl glucuronide by UGT1A9 is documented in human hepatocytes/microsomes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15370961/) without established human DILI causation.

Active anti-aromatase metabolite with intrinsic androgenic activity; LiverTox (NBK548926) notes rare cholestatic DILI is likely an idiosyncratic reaction to an uncharacterized CYP3A4 metabolite.

Discontinued in Phase I due to dose-limiting liver enzyme elevations and low bioavailability; major human metabolite BIBU1476 is pharmacologically inactive and not established as hepatotoxic.
Four pharmacologically active hydroxy metabolites circulate at much lower levels than parent; LiverTox (NBK548645) notes hepatotoxicity mechanism is unestablished.

injury_mechanism: Atropaldehyde is a highly reactive electrophilic metabolite that covalently binds cellular proteins and depletes glutathione, triggering direct cytotoxicity and/or immune-mediated hepatic necrosis.
notes: Well-documented reactive metabolite linked to felbamate-induced acute liver failure and aplastic anemia.

metabolite_name: Fenclozic acid acyl glucuronide and CYP-derived oxidative reactive metabolites
injury_mechanism: Reactive acyl glucuronide, acyl-CoA thioester, and CYP-mediated oxidative intermediates covalently bind hepatic proteins and deplete glutathione, causing hepatocellular and cholestatic injury.
notes: Withdrawn for human jaundice/hepatotoxicity; mechanistic covalent binding and metabolite profiles characterized in chimeric humanized-liver mice and rodents.
Excreted mainly as fenoprofen glucuronide and 4'-hydroxyfenoprofen glucuronide (DailyMed); LiverTox states mechanism of rare idiosyncratic DILI is unknown.

injury_mechanism: FIAU-TP competitively inhibits mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma and incorporates into mtDNA, causing severe mtDNA depletion, lactic acidosis, microvesicular steatosis, and liver failure.
notes: Active antiviral triphosphate metabolite directly causes lethal human mitochondrial hepatotoxicity.
Discontinued in clinical development; no well-documented active or hepatotoxic human metabolites identified in published literature.
Prodrug activated by sphingosine kinase to modulate S1P receptors; mechanism of fingolimod-induced liver injury is unknown per LiverTox (NBK548384).

injury_mechanism: CYP-mediated demethylenation forms a catechol that oxidizes to a reactive ortho-quinone, which covalently binds hepatic proteins and depletes glutathione, leading to centrilobular hepatic necrosis.
notes: Reactive ortho-quinone intermediates trapped in human and animal liver microsomes; drug withdrawn due to fulminant hepatitis (PMID 1506632).
Cleared primarily unchanged by renal excretion (DailyMed); mechanism of idiosyncratic fluconazole hepatotoxicity is unknown.

injury_mechanism: Inhibits hepatic bile salt export (taurocholate efflux/BSEP) in human hepatocytes alongside parent flutamide.
notes: Major active antiandrogen metabolite; less directly cytotoxic than parent flutamide in rat hepatocytes in vitro, though both inhibit BSEP (pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/tx7001542).

metabolite_name: CYP-derived electrophilic reactive metabolites (e.g. N-hydroxy/nitroso intermediates)
injury_mechanism: Bioactivation by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 produces electrophilic intermediates that covalently bind microsomal proteins, deplete glutathione, and aggravate mitochondrial complex I inhibition and ATP depletion.
notes: Implicated in severe and fatal hepatocellular injury (LiverTox NBK548908).

injury_mechanism: See phenytoin arene oxide metabolite below.
notes: Water-soluble prodrug rapidly converted by phosphatases to active anticonvulsant phenytoin.

injury_mechanism: Reactive arene oxide intermediates covalently bind cellular macromolecules and act as haptens, triggering immunoallergic hepatotoxicity (often within DRESS/anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome).
notes: Formed from the active metabolite phenytoin; well-established cause of severe idiosyncratic DILI (LiverTox NBK547879).
Major active metabolite in fecal extracts (14% of dose).

injury_mechanism: CYP1A1 and CYP3A4 catalyze oxidative defluorination to a para-hydroxyaniline intermediate that oxidizes to a reactive quinone-imine, forming covalent GSH/protein adducts.
notes: Bioactivation demonstrated in human hepatic and pulmonary microsomes; LiverTox (NBK548839) notes a toxic or immunogenic intermediate is suspected.
Active intracellular metabolites mediating ribonucleotide reductase inhibition and DNA incorporation; LiverTox (NBK548575) notes rare DILI mechanism is unestablished.

injury_mechanism: Acyl glucuronide is oxidized by CYP2C8 to a benzyl radical intermediate that covalently binds CYP2C8 heme, causing irreversible mechanism-based enzyme inactivation and clinical DDIs.
notes: Clinically important hepatic enzyme inactivator; LiverTox (NBK547926) notes rare clinical DILI is likely an immunologic response to a metabolic intermediate.

injury_mechanism: Released calicheamicin binds DNA and induces double-stranded DNA breaks and apoptosis in CD33-expressing hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells, causing sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS/VOD).
notes: Cytotoxic ADC payload responsible for both antileukemic efficacy and severe/fatal hepatic SOS.
Active analgesic metabolite formed by esterase hydrolysis; subsequently bioactivated by CYPs.

injury_mechanism: CYP-catalyzed 5-hydroxylation followed by two-electron oxidation generates electrophilic para-quinone imines that form covalent GSH/protein adducts.
notes: Demonstrated in human liver microsomes; glafenine was withdrawn due to severe hepatotoxicity and anaphylaxis.

injury_mechanism: Inhibits ferrochelatase, causing hepatic accumulation of protoporphyrin IX (PPIX), bile duct blockage, and disrupted bile acid homeostasis.
notes: Flagged: mechanism established in mice and precipitates acute porphyric hepatotoxicity in humans; LiverTox (NBK548177) notes mechanism of rare non-porphyric cholestatic DILI is unknown.
Contributes to fetal hemoglobin induction in sickle cell disease; LiverTox (NBK548724) states rare hydroxyurea hepatitis is likely hypersensitivity-mediated with no established toxic metabolite.
Active dihydrodiol metabolite with ~15-fold lower BTK inhibitory activity than ibrutinib; LiverTox (NBK548449) notes rare DILI mechanism is unclear.

injury_mechanism: Labile acyl glucuronide undergoes spontaneous acyl migration and reacts with nucleophilic protein groups via transacylation or glycation, forming covalent hepatic protein adducts.
notes: Withdrawn from market due to severe hepatotoxicity; acyl glucuronide is notably unstable and reactive.

injury_mechanism: Not established as hepatotoxic; LiverTox notes imatinib DILI is likely immune-mediated or due to HBV reactivation.
notes: Similar in vitro potency to parent with longer half-life (~40 h vs ~18 h); no hepatotoxic metabolite identified in LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547959/).

injury_mechanism: Proposed covalent binding of reactive acyl glucuronide to hepatic proteins, triggering immune-mediated or idiosyncratic liver injury.
notes: LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548001/) states mechanism is unknown but likely mediated by a toxic metabolic intermediate; direct human DILI causality for indomethacin acyl glucuronide is proposed rather than definitively established.

injury_mechanism: Monoclonal antibody not metabolized by the liver; DILI occurs via autoimmune/immunomodulatory mechanisms or HBV reactivation.
notes: Catabolized proteolytically rather than by hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes.

notes: No hepatic metabolism or toxic metabolite.

injury_mechanism: Hydrolysis to N-isopropylhydrazine followed by CYP oxidation to reactive diazonium/isopropyl radicals that covalently bind hepatic proteins and cause necrosis.
notes: Withdrawn due to severe human hepatotoxicity; note that isopropylhydrazine is a primary hepatotoxin in rats and its exact reactive metabolite role in humans remains unclear.

injury_mechanism: Reactive intermediate formed via 5-hydroxylation irreversibly and covalently binds hepatic microsomal proteins, proposed to trigger allergic/idiosyncratic hepatitis.
notes: Covalent binding demonstrated in both human and mouse liver microsomes (NADPH/O2-dependent, inhibited by piperonyl butoxide); exact chemical structure uncharacterized.

injury_mechanism: CYP2E1 oxidizes acetylhydrazine and hydrazine into reactive intermediates causing oxidative stress and covalent macromolecular binding in hepatocytes.
notes: Source disagreement: Metushi et al. 2016 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4876174/) argue earlier rat studies misattributed toxicity to acetylhydrazine/hydrazine and that direct bioactivation of parent isoniazid forming covalent lysine adducts drives human immune-mediated IDILI.

injury_mechanism: UNKNOWN; LiverTox notes transient ALT elevations occur by an unknown mechanism.
notes: Major circulating metabolite (~3.4x parent exposure at steady state, t1/2 24 h) with in vitro retinoid activity of unknown clinical significance; also interconverts with tretinoin.

injury_mechanism: Not established as hepatotoxic; LiverTox notes mechanism of idiosyncratic DILI is unknown.
notes: Comparable antifungal activity to parent (trough concentration ~2x parent); no hepatotoxic metabolite established.

injury_mechanism: DAK is further oxidized by FMO to a reactive dialdehyde (plus piperazine iminium ions) that causes covalent binding and direct hepatocellular cytotoxicity.

injury_mechanism: Forms a reactive intermediate trapped as a glutathione conjugate in human and rat hepatocytes that causes cytotoxicity.
notes: LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547846/) attributes DILI to metabolic idiosyncrasy; flagged because cytotoxicity/SULT-inhibition protection was shown in rat hepatocytes/in vitro and human DILI causality is not clinically confirmed.

injury_mechanism: Shunted to CYP bioactivation when UGT glucuronidation is inhibited (e.g. by valproate); the reactive arene oxide covalently binds proteins/DNA/RNA triggering DRESS/hypersensitivity and liver injury.
notes: Supported by LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548562/) linking hypersensitivity/immunoallergic hepatotoxicity to reactive arene oxide intermediates.

metabolite_name: O-dealkylated lapatinib (GW690006) quinone imine, reactive aldehydes, and quinone methides
injury_mechanism: CYP3A4/5 oxidation of O-dealkylated lapatinib and fluorobenzyl cleavage generate reactive quinone imines and aldehydes that covalently modify proteins and trigger HLA-DQA1*02:01-linked immune liver injury.
notes: Supported by LiverTox (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547971/) implicating toxic/immunogenic metabolic intermediates in HLA-associated hepatotoxicity.
